title: podman-restart service delays user's systemd critical chain even when no containers have been created
body:
### Issue Description

Podman has the **podman-restart** service which starts containers on boot if they were supposed to, but even if no containers exist, the service takes a significant time.

If I add `ExecCondition=/usr/bin/sh -c 'if [ -z "$(/usr/bin/podman ps -aq)" ]; then exit 1; fi'`, the delay doesn't happen; which means `/usr/bin/podman $LOGGING start --all --filter should-start-on-boot=true` is using more time than the needed for checking and exiting if there is nothing to do:
- `podman-restart.service @733ms +2.837s` No containers
- `podman.service @741ms +121ms` No containers + ExecCondition

### Steps to reproduce the issue

Steps to reproduce the issue
1. Install podman 
2. Enable systemd services (user)
3. Check `systemd-analyze --user critical-chain`


### Describe the results you received

A significant delay exists even if the service doesn't have anything to start

### Describe the results you expected

Almost no delay if no containers need to start

comments.body:
The first podman command after boot has to do a lot more in general and will always be slower, the amount can depend on many factors.
First, it needs to restet the state of all containers, i.e. several database writes, then it also may need to cleanup removed containers, see https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/issues/29109.
Second, as rootless we also need to rexec into the user namespace.

However that should be only the first command after boot, if you add `/usr/bin/podman ps -aq` before that I would expect that delay to end up there? Is the exec condition timing in that case attributed to the unit correctly?
If you have all the services disabled you should be able to correctly measure the different time of the command after each boot with `time podman ...`. It would be interesting to know if really on start takes longer.

The time of the original machine service dropped to 800ms and I wasn't able to reproduce the 2.8s, so I reproduced it on a clean install in a VM in a different host (more powerful than the real original machine so time varies).

I replaced the ExecStart to get the same context for the measurements and I got this:

but when I tried both time ps -aq and time [start...] as the ExecStart I got similar times of about 0.8s. Maybe the ExecCondition doesn't count as delay for systemd?
